value.approach: Analyze churn by plan and over time, then investigate customer-level churn rates to identify whether differences are driven by plan-specific factors, customer acquisition quality, or customer value mix.

steps.question: How does monthly churn_mrr trend over 2024 by plan, and what percentage of monthly new_mrr does each plan lose to churn?
steps.rationale: Establish churn patterns by product segment (plan) and quantify revenue efficiency. The anomalous positive correlations with growth metrics suggest the real story is revenue retention by plan, not absolute churn volume.

steps.question: What is the per-customer churn rate (churn_mrr / customers) by plan and month, and how does it correlate with ARPU within each plan?
steps.rationale: Investigate whether churn is driven by losing more customers (volume effect), losing higher-value customers (ARPU quality effect), or plan-specific cohort behavior. This reveals the mechanism: are we acquiring low-fit customers, or do all plans have structural churn issues?

props.title: Per-Customer Churn Rate by Plan Over Time
Churn Rate vs ARPU by Plan

props.content: Churn rate heterogeneity across plans is statistically anova-tested (p = 2.09e-22), with Enterprise showing the highest per-customer churn and Pro the lowest; the overall ARPU–churn correlation (r = 0.974) indicates whether losing higher-value customers or volume is the primary driver.

Plan churn rates are significantly heterogeneous (p=4.65e-18, anova), spanning 8.5 pp — Starter leads at 17.17% vs. Enterprise at 8.67% — while overall churn MRR trends rising, peaking in 2024-12 and sitting 0% below that peak as of 2024-12.
What drives churn in this data?

Overall churn MRR trended rising across 2024, with the late-year median (21550) running 1.5× the early-year median (13950); plan-level churn rates are statistically heterogeneous (p=4.65e-18, anova), with Starter averaging 17.17% vs Enterprise at 8.67% (Step 1). Per-customer churn MRR is also significantly different across plans (Step 2), and a step-change in churn MRR per customer was detected at 2024-04; however, ARPU does not vary month-to-month within plans, so the ARPU–churn correlation is cross-sectional (between plans) rather than within-plan (Steps 1, 2).

props.label: Step 1 — Monthly churn MRR trend by plan and churn rate as % of new MRR

props.title: Churn rate % of new MRR by plan

props.content: Churn MRR trended rising overall (slope 1207.3427 $/month), while churn rate trended rising; plan churn rates differ significantly (anova p=4.65e-18) across a 8.5 pp range, pointing to plan mix as a primary lever (Step 1).

props.label: Step 2 — Per-customer churn MRR by plan and ARPU correlation

props.title: Churn MRR per customer by plan over time
Churn MRR per customer vs ARPU (by plan)

props.content: Step 1 showed plan-level churn rates are structurally different, suggesting plan composition — not random customer loss — as the driver; Step 2 confirms per-customer churn MRR is also plan-heterogeneous (p=2.09e-22), with a step-change at 2024-04. Because ARPU does not vary within plans month-to-month, the ARPU–churn correlation (Pearson r=0.974) is a between-plan signal: higher-ARPU plans lose more revenue per customer lost, not that within a plan high-ARPU months churn more (Steps 1, 2).

The dominant churn driver is plan tier: Starter consistently churns at the highest rate and loses the most revenue per customer, while Enterprise is most retentive. The step-change in per-customer churn at 2024-04 is the sharpest intervention point to investigate — examine what changed in that cohort's acquisition, onboarding, or pricing at that date. Recommended next steps: 1 drill into the Starter segment by acquisition channel and tenure to test whether this is a fit or onboarding problem, and (2) model retention by cohort-month to distinguish structural plan churn from period-specific shocks.
